strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated question: how much repo-level editing capability can be internalized via training signals rather than inference-time scaffolding. The 'noise–validity gap' framing of GitHub PRs (Table 2) is informative.

The data pipeline is unusually rigorous: round-trip verification of Search/Replace blocks against a reconstructed ground-truth 'after' state (Algorithm 1), uniqueness/non-overlap checks, and a multi-layered decontamination protocol (repository blocklists, exact file hashing, 15-gram and Jaccard checks) go beyond typical practice for web-crawled code corpora.

The resulting corpus (2M verified PRs, 17.7B tokens, 12 languages, 45k repos) is claimed to be the largest publicly released PR-derived dataset explicitly built and verified for repo-level mid-training, which is a useful community contribution; detailed release schema and processing specs (Appendix A) support reproducibility.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough for this type of work: ablations disentangle mid-training vs. SFT, edit format (Table 8 shows diffs vs. S/R is decisive: 27.8 → 24.4 on Verified), issue augmentation, and error-driven augmentation (Table 9). The unified-diff degradation result is a concrete, actionable finding.

Results are strong in context: 24.3% Lite / 30.6% Verified with a 32B model under a simplified Agentless protocol surpasses 72B open systems and SWE-Gym with an OpenHands scaffold, supporting the central claim that capability can be baked into weights.

The generalization analysis (Figure 2: HumanEval and LiveCodeBench improving during mid-training rather than degrading) and the Pass@k analysis (Figure 3) add useful insight beyond the headline numbers.

Hyperparameters, prompts, inference settings, and training costs are reported in detail (Appendices C–D), and limitations (single base model, cost of scaling, no agentic evaluation) are acknowledged honestly in Appendix D.
weaknesses: Single-base-model evidence: all results are on Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. The central claim—that repository editing capability is encoded into weights via Clean-PR—is supported by one model/one scale, so generalization of the recipe is unverified. The authors attribute this to compute cost, but it materially weakens the claim's reach.

Potential train/eval contamination in the SFT stage is not fully resolved. The Origin SFT trajectories are derived from SWE-bench-Live and SWE-Gym; SWE-Gym tasks come from SWE-bench repositories, and the relationship between these trajectories and SWE-bench Lite/Verified instances (which originate from the same 12 repositories) deserves explicit, per-instance decontamination evidence rather than a decontamination protocol applied only to the mid-training corpus. The 15-gram/Jaccard checks are described for the mid-training data.

The external baseline comparison (Table 7) copies numbers from original papers, so scaffolds, inference budgets, and decoding settings differ across rows; the headline 'outperforms 72B systems' comparison is therefore not a controlled experiment. The internal StarCoder2-style baseline is the more reliable comparison, and while useful, it differs from Clean-PR in three ways at once (format, filtering, issue context), with only partial disentangling via Table 8 on the Python subset.

Several filtering components are heuristic and potentially brittle: bot detection via username regexes, issue linking via prioritized regular expressions, title/description blocklists. There is no reported human validation or precision/recall estimate of the issue-linking or bot-filtering stages, so the quality of the 'issue-augmented intent' signal is asserted rather than measured.

Novelty is modest on the method side: Search/Replace edit blocks, Agentless-style decomposition, and negative/contrastive SFT examples are all established techniques; the contribution is primarily a carefully engineered dataset and training recipe. This is legitimate, but the paper's framing as a new paradigm somewhat overstates it.

The +5.7% HumanEval improvement from mid-training on PR data is surprising and is presented without error bars, seeds, or variance estimates anywhere in the paper; given 300/500-instance benchmarks, differences of a few points (e.g., 24.3 vs. 20.4) may not be statistically robust.

Only functional SWE-bench results are reported for the final model; evaluation on out-of-domain agentic or multilingual SWE benchmarks (e.g., Multi-SWE-bench, SWE-PolyBench) is absent despite the multi-language corpus being a selling point, so the claimed benefit of language diversity rests on a single aggregate comparison.

License/attribution compliance for the released dataset is discussed only at a high level in the impact statement; per-repository licensing status is not described in the release specification (Table 16).

strengths: The core resource contribution is substantial: a 2M-instance verified PR corpus (17.7B tokens) with deterministic round-trip verification of Search/Replace blocks (Algorithm 1), which is a genuinely useful and largely missing data asset for repo-level editing (Table 1 shows the scale gap vs. prior corpora).

The decontamination protocol is unusually thorough for a data-centric paper: repository-level exclusion plus SHA-256 file matching and 15-gram/Jaccard content-level checks against SWE-bench gold patches and issue texts (Appendix A.6).

The paper disentangles its pipeline components rather than presenting a monolithic system: Table 8 isolates edit format and issue linking, Table 9 isolates error-driven augmentation, and a carefully constructed StarCoder2-style baseline (Appendix B) with matched token budget (17.4B vs 17.7B) supports the claim that data quality, not just volume, drives gains.

Reported gains are large and internally consistent across two benchmark splits (24.3% Lite / 30.6% Verified), with intermediate metrics (Valid Patch Rate, File Acc., Line Acc.) that plausibly trace the mechanism (verified S/R format raises validity 89.7%→96.3%).
Reproducibility is addressed in detail: full hyperparameters, prompts, filtering rules, dataset schema, and an explicit data release specification (Tables 16-20, Appendix A.9).
weaknesses: Cross-system comparisons are confounded by scaffold differences. Table 7 compares Clean-PR (Agentless) against SWE-Gym (OpenHands agent) and 72B systems (Lingma-SWE, SWE-Fixer) whose numbers are copied from other papers under different scaffolds and possibly different evaluation dates/harnesses. The claim of 'outperforming complex agentic frameworks and larger models' is therefore not apples-to-apples and is overstated relative to the evidence.

All experiments use a single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B). The central claim that repository-level capability 'can be encoded directly into model weights' via this pipeline is demonstrated on exactly one architecture/size, and the authors acknowledge this only in Appendix D. Generalisation of the recipe is unverified.

No statistical treatment. SWE-bench Lite/Verified are 300/500 instances, decoding is greedy, and no confidence intervals, seed variance, or significance tests are reported; several headline gaps (e.g., 24.3% vs 22.3% Lite; 27.8% vs 27.4% Verified for error augmentation) may not be meaningful at this sample size.

The mid-training evaluation is only on Python benchmarks (SWE-bench), so the 'benefits of multi-language training' claim rests on aggregate Pass@1 improvements on Python tasks alone; no non-Python evaluation (e.g., Multi-SWE-bench) is provided to substantiate the abstraction-transfer argument.

Filter precision is under-validated. The noise taxonomy (Table 2) and filters (username-regex bot detection, extension rules, title/description blocklists) are heuristic; the paper reports corpus statistics but no human-audited estimate of how much residual noise or how much genuine signal the pipeline discards. The suspicious claim that mid-training *improves* HumanEval by +5.7 points over the base model deserves closer scrutiny or controls.

The 'internalisation vs. scaffolding' framing is only partially tested: the SFT stage uses trajectories derived from SWE-bench-adjacent resources (SWE-rebench, SWE-Gym), so attributing the full gap between Base+SFT and Clean-PR-mid-trained models specifically to PR-derived mid-training data (rather than data volume or composition) could be tighter.

Reproducibility of the corpus itself is limited: the 8.6TB crawl and crawl dates are not specified, and while a release is promised, neither code nor data is available at review time, so the pipeline cannot currently be independently verified.

strengths: Substantial and useful resource contribution: the Clean-PR corpus (2M verified PRs across 12 languages, 17.7B tokens) addresses a genuine gap between small, executable SWE-bench-style datasets and large but unstructured natural code corpora. The round-trip verification of Search/Replace blocks (bit-wise reconstruction checks, Algorithm 1) is a well-motivated quality mechanism.

Careful data engineering is documented in depth: noise taxonomy with statistics (Table 2), explicit core-extension filtering rules (Table 12), issue-linking regexes, context windowing, and a multi-layered decontamination protocol (repo exclusion, SHA-256 file matching, n-gram/Jaccard overlap filtering). This transparency supports reproducibility.

Reasonably thorough ablations: the paper disentangles edit format vs. linked-issue context (Table 8), quantifies error-driven augmentation (Table 9), and constructs a controlled StarCoder2-style baseline at matched token budget rather than only citing external numbers.

Interesting and practically relevant findings: mid-training alone provides most of the gain; verified Search/Replace training improves valid patch rate and line localisation over unified diffs; and Figure 2 provides evidence that the data format affects catastrophic forgetting (diffs degrade HumanEval, verified S/R improves it).

Honest limitations discussion (Appendix D) acknowledging single-model scope, absence of agentic-loop evaluation, and compute constraints; impact statement addresses security/licensing concerns appropriately.
weaknesses: Key claims rest on narrow evaluation. Despite the multi-language framing, all results are on SWE-bench Lite (300) and Verified (500) — Python-only benchmarks — and the paper does not evaluate on Multi-SWE-bench or SWE-PolyBench, where the claimed cross-lingual transfer benefit could actually be tested. The interpretation that Java/C++/Go exposure 'enhances abstract reasoning' is speculative without multilingual evaluation.

No statistical rigor around small evaluation sets: no variance, seeds, or confidence intervals are reported for differences of 2–4 points on 300/500 instances, which are within plausible run-to-run noise for SWE-bench.

External comparisons (Table 7) copy results from original papers obtained with different scaffolds and inference budgets, so the 'outperforms 72B models' claim is not an apples-to-apples comparison; only the internal ablation comparisons are controlled.

The dataset is promised but not yet released at review time; all reproducibility claims hinge on this future release. Additionally, mid-training data and SFT trajectories both derive from GitHub PR mining (SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym), and potential overlap between the mid-training corpus and SFT data sources is not analyzed.

Single base model (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B): the central claim that repo-level capability 'can be internalised into model weights' is validated on one architecture only, and the confound between base-model priors and the data recipe cannot be excluded.

Potential train/test workflow leakage: the SFT data is constructed by decomposing ground-truth repairs from SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym into oracle localisation/navigation targets, and evaluation uses the same decomposed Agentless protocol; gains from training on oracle-decomposed trajectories may partially reflect task-format alignment rather than intrinsic editing capability.

Some sloppiness undermines confidence: Table 2's 'Clean' and 'Total' ratios are hard to interpret with non-exclusive categories; minor typos ('OpenHand', 'besides heavy agent scaffolding'); the abstract's headline framing (13.6%/12.3% gains) conflates the full three-stage pipeline with the data contribution that is the paper's core novelty.

strengths: The data construction pipeline is rigorous and well-documented: round-trip Search/Replace verification (Algorithm 1), minimal-unique-context derivation, multi-layer decontamination (repo blocklisting, SHA-256 exact matching, 15-gram and Jaccard filtering), and an unusually thorough semantic leakage analysis (Table 16) showing no correlation between train-test similarity and resolve rate (r=-0.061, p=0.184). This substantially strengthens the credibility of the headline claims.

The corpus itself (2M verified PRs across 12 languages, 17.7B tokens) with detailed schema and release specifications is a concrete, reusable community contribution that fills a real gap between noisy commit corpora and small executable SWE datasets (Table 1).

The experimental design is largely well-controlled for the central claim: a StarCoder2-style baseline built on the same 16.4M raw PRs, matched token budgets (17.4B vs 17.7B), and ablations that separately isolate edit format (Table 8) and error-driven augmentation (Table 9).

The error-driven augmentation for hard negatives and distractor regions is a sensible and validated mechanism against over-editing, with consistent gains in both localisation metrics and end-to-end resolution (Table 9).

Generality is probed beyond the main setting: 7B scale transfer (Table 10), multilingual evaluation on Multi-SWE-bench Flash (Table 11), and transfer back into an agentic OpenHands scaffold (Table 12), which supports the claim that capability is internalised in weights rather than scaffold-specific.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix D) and an impact statement addressing code-generation reliability, misuse, and licensing are present.
weaknesses: No statistical treatment of results: single runs with no variance estimates, seeds, or significance tests. While the headline gains are large, several ablation deltas (e.g., 24.3 vs 27.8 on a 300-instance Lite split) are within plausible run-to-run noise ranges, and the paper provides no mechanism to assess this.

Some external comparisons in Table 7 are apples-to-oranges: SWE-Gym, Lingma-SWE, and SWE-Fixer use different scaffolds, training data sources, and possibly evaluation protocols. The claim that a 32B model 'surpasses 72B baselines' is stated without controlling for these confounds, and the paper's own reasoning (scaffolds matter greatly) undermines direct cross-paper comparisons.

The SFT-only baseline in Table 6 is surprisingly weak (11.3% Lite, below the Instruct model on Verified at some points), raising questions about whether it was tuned to a comparable strength; the strongest evidence for the mid-training stage would come from a longer/more carefully tuned SFT-only control.

The SFT trajectories derive from SWE-rebench and SWE-Gym, whose instances are themselves harvested from live GitHub PRs; although decontamination is addressed for Clean-PR mid-training data, the analogous decontamination for the SFT trajectory data is less clearly documented, which matters for the Verified/Lite results.

Novelty is moderate: the individual components (Agentless-style stepwise SFT, Search/Replace formats, issue-linking, negative augmentation) are established; the contribution is primarily careful large-scale data engineering plus an integration, which is valuable but not a fundamentally new method or insight.

Some methodological details are under-specified or heuristic: bot detection via username regex, issue linking via regex patterns (false-positive issue links are not quantified), and hard-negative generation by an intermediate model without reporting how many generated negatives were validated or how noisy they are.

Dataset release is only 'planned'; reproducibility currently rests on descriptions rather than released artefacts, and there is no released code for the pipeline or inference scaffold at submission time.

strengths: Well-motivated research question: the paper isolates how much repo-level editing capability can be internalized into weights rather than scaffolded at inference time, a question that is genuinely underexplored.

The verified Search/Replace conversion pipeline (Algorithm 1) is a concrete, checkable contribution: round-trip patch application with bitwise reconstruction, minimal unique context expansion, and non-overlap checks give the corpus a falsifiable quality guarantee rather than heuristic filtering alone.

Decontamination is treated seriously and multi-layered: repository blocklisting, SHA-256 file matching, 15-gram filtering, issue Jaccard filtering, plus a semantic leakage analysis (Table 16) that actually reports a null result (r=-0.061, n.s.) instead of only asserting cleanliness.

Internal ablations are fairly well controlled: Table 8 disentangles edit format (S/R vs diff) from issue augmentation on the same data source, and Table 9 isolates the error-driven augmentation on top of identical SFT data, so the mid-training contribution (Table 6) is interpretable.

Broad generalization coverage: 7B scale transfer (Table 10), multilingual Multi-SWE-bench Flash (Table 11), and agentic OpenHands transfer (Table 12) support the claim that the capability is encoded in weights rather than tied to one scaffold.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong for a systems paper: full training hyperparameters (Table 21), exact inference prompts (Tables 22-24), the StarCoder2-style baseline construction (Appendix B), and a dataset release schema (Table 20) are specified.
weaknesses: Potential leakage in the SFT stage is not addressed with the same rigor as the mid-training corpus. The stepwise SFT data is drawn from SWE-rebench and SWE-Gym trajectories, which are SWE-bench-derived task distributions; the semantic leakage analysis (Appendix A.7) only embeds Clean-PR-train against SWE-bench Verified, not the SFT trajectories. The no-overlap claim is made explicitly only for Multi-SWE-bench-RL.

Headline gains are single-run numbers with no variance estimates or significance testing; several margins (e.g., 24.3 vs 22.3 on Lite between full and Python-only settings; augmentation gains of ~2-4 points) could be within run-to-run noise, especially on 300-500 instance benchmarks.

External comparisons (Table 7) copy numbers from original papers using different scaffolds (OpenHands, SWE-SynInfer, SWE-Fixer), so claims like 'surpassing the 72B baselines' confound scaffold, decoding budget, and training recipe; the paper acknowledges the scaffold difference but the SOTA-adjacent framing overstates what this comparison supports.

The StarCoder2-style baseline differs from Clean-PR in filtering, format, and issue integration simultaneously; while Table 8 partially disentangles these, the baseline is constructed by the authors rather than reproducing any published pipeline, weakening the 'prevailing standard' framing.

The corpus is described as 'the largest publicly released' yet is only planned for release; no artifact link or anonymized repository is provided, so verifiability of the central dataset claims currently rests entirely on the paper's description.

The multi-language contribution is under-supported by its own evidence: the Python-only model (3.8B tokens) already achieves 27.8 vs 30.6 Verified, and the explanation for cross-lingual gains ('enhances abstract reasoning') is speculative; the cost-benefit (259h vs 60h training) is not analyzed.

The Valid Patch Rate metric (77% -> 96%) is partly an artifact of the S/R format matching the evaluation scaffold itself, since patches are applied via the same string-replacement mechanism used in training; the paper would benefit from also reporting performance under an orthogonal patch format.

Inference uses top-3 file retrieval and greedy decoding; sensitivity of the reported Pass@1 to these scaffold choices (e.g., top-k retrieval width) is unexplored despite the scaffold being a shared component across all rows of Table 6.

strengths: Substantial and novel data contribution: Clean-PR converts ~16.4M raw GitHub PRs into a verified 2M-instance Search/Replace corpus (17.7B tokens) with a round-trip patch-application verification (Algorithm 1), making it arguably the largest verified PR-derived editing corpus; the release plan with detailed schema (Table 20) supports reproducibility.

Careful ablation design: the paper disentangles format (S/R vs. diff), context (linked issue vs. PR description), mid-training vs. SFT-only, token-matched StarCoder2-style baseline, error-driven augmentation, and language scope (Tables 6, 8, 9), which strengthens causal attribution of the gains.

Strong contamination hygiene: repository exclusion, SHA-256 matching, 15-gram and Jaccard filtering, plus an embedding-based semantic leakage analysis (Table 16) with a negative correlation result — this goes beyond standard practice and is a model for the field.

Breadth of evaluation beyond the headline result: 7B scale generalisation (Table 10), multilingual evaluation on Multi-SWE-bench Flash (Table 11), transfer into OpenHands agentic evaluation (Table 12), Pass@k scaling, and HumanEval/LiveCodeBench retention analysis (Figure 2) all support the central claim that repo-level capability is internalised in the weights.
Honest limitations discussion (Appendix D) about the ≤5-core-file filter, long-tail edits, and backbone generality.
weaknesses: Baseline strength concerns: the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct zero-shot result (10.7 Lite / 18.3 Verified) appears low relative to published Agentless-style results for this model (typically ~30% on Verified with retrieval scaffolds), raising the possibility that the headline gains (+13.6/+12.3) are partly inflated by an under-tuned scaffold or an apples-to-oranges inference protocol; the paper does not reconcile this with prior reported numbers.

No statistical significance testing or multi-seed variance for any benchmark; SWE-bench Lite has only 300 instances and several claimed gains (e.g., Error Aug 21.8→24.3 Lite, +2.5) are within plausible run-to-run noise, weakening some quantitative conclusions.

Table 7 external comparison is problematic: SWE-Fixer and Lingma-SWE are reported with identical numbers (22.0/30.2), suggesting a copying error, and the comparison conflates different frameworks and evaluation settings rather than a controlled setup.

The intermediate-metric definitions (Line Accuracy) are imprecisely specified, and the SFT origin data (SWE-rebench/SWE-Gym trajectories) introduces a potential confound when attributing gains to Clean-PR mid-training, since the SFT distribution itself carries repository-level supervision.

Dataset and code are 'planned' for release rather than released at review time, limiting reproducibility of the central artefact; greedy-decoding-only main results also exclude any variance information.
Minor presentation issues: duplicated regex patterns in bot filtering (bot$ repeated), inconsistent notation, and some figure text (e.g., Figure 1) is dense and hard to parse.
